column2: Cage gives a formal course on the structure of music and choreography; he is also asked to give concerts of modern music, which he decides to devote almost entirely to Erik Satie. a single concert reserved for Cage's own compositions Consequences: The birth of the Satie festival and of the production of The Ruse of Medusa

Cage divides Satie's work (about thirteen hours of music, excluding “Vexations” and “Furniture Music,” which he does not yet have) into twenty-five half-hour concerts, three evenings a week after dinner, in chronological order. He usually plays in the dining hall, sometimes on the piano in his cottage, with the windows open so that the audience can settle on the lawn. He names the series the “Amateur Music Festival,” since he is not a very good pianist and Satie is very simple. When other instruments are required (rarely), he recruits talent from the community. 25 half-hour concerts, 3 evenings a week, after the evening meal; ~13 hours of music; windows open, the audience on the lawn Consequences: Part of the community irritated by the Satie monograph

To soothe the irritation and make the series reasonable, Albers requires Cage to give a ten-minute talk before each concert, placing Satie in the modern context. Albers himself is not irritated: he is responsive to Cage's thinking about the opposition, yet fusion, of form and content. A 10-minute talk before each concert Consequences: The talks go well until the anti-Beethoven speech

Around the middle of the series, to set out Satie's position (anti-Beethoven), Cage gives a long talk denouncing Beethoven. Bodky, who is teaching the Beethoven sonatas that summer, responds with a concert of Beethoven's late quartets, preceded by a talk against those who disparage Beethoven. Cage replies that he did not mean to hurt anyone: he and most modern composers draw their inspiration from Satie (and Bach), not from Beethoven. a concert of Beethoven's late quartets by Bodky Consequences: An escalation of the conflict, resolved by Levi's farce

At lunch, Levi taps his glass and announces, very seriously, that so grave a division has arisen in the faculty that no normal means can resolve it: he proposes, in his capacity as rector, a duel to the death — the Beethovenians armed with cold Wiener schnitzels, the Satieists with flaming crêpes Suzette. A food fight actually breaks out, and some thirty people come out of it rather soiled; the argument dies down, but a few go on speaking of Cage's “desecration” of the musical heritage. a glass tapped at lunch; cold Wiener schnitzels against flaming crêpes Suzette; ~30 people soiled Consequences: The conflict deflated

M.C. spends the beginning of the summer at the Rondthalers' on Ocracoke Island translating Satie's play; she comes back with the translation toward the end of the summer. Cage finds it very beautiful. Cage had discovered the play in a limited edition illustrated by Georges Braque, in the rare book collection of the New York Public Library. a limited edition illustrated by Georges Braque; the music of the play printed in the volume; Cage already had the score from another source Consequences: The translation ready for the production

The play had been performed only once before, in France, with Mme Darius Milhaud in the principal female role. Cage gives this role to Elaine de Kooning; Fuller plays Baron Méduse; Isaac Rosenfeld and Alvin Charles Few (nephew of the Black cook Malrey Few) take small parts; Cunningham dances and choreographs the mechanical monkey, for which Lippold designs a tail (which Cunningham still keeps hanging in his studio). De Kooning makes the set sketches, Elaine carries them out and enriches them with students. the mechanical monkey's tail designed by Lippold, kept by Cunningham Consequences: A production that will become a mythical founding event

The text is thin and hard to make coherent. Fuller memorizes it easily (at Harvard one had to learn half of Shakespeare by heart) but refuses to act: he wants to do his own thinking, not someone else's lines. Arthur Penn, there all summer but busy writing his own play, is called in; he agrees to step in and imposes firm direction, adding improvisation to the skeleton of the text — a mixture of text and happening, but distinctly directed, controlled, tied to the music. Consequences: The show takes shape; Penn's theatrical awakening

Rehearsals are open (the college believes one can watch the process, not only the result); one day of heavy attendance, Fuller confides to Penn that he is afraid of making a fool of himself. Penn devises exercises in which the two of them deliberately make fools of themselves: hopping about, doing crazy things, laughing artificially, rolling on the floor. It becomes fun, then liberating, then inventive — and Fuller blossoms. hopping, artificial laughter, rolling on the floor Consequences: Fuller plays Baron Méduse magnificently, according to Cage

The performance, with no known detractor, is unanimously considered the high point of a remarkable summer. Cage: Fuller plays magnificently. Fuller will later say that all his success as a lecturer came from having been Baron Méduse, and that Arthur Penn did him one of the greatest services of his life by setting him free on the stage — it helped his thinking-out-loud sessions. Consequences: A founding myth of “mixed media”; Fuller the lecturer set free

The participants seriously consider staging the play in New York in the fall, but none of them has any power on the New York stage: impossible to raise the money, find the place, organize it. They nonetheless take away all the sets, costumes, and what Bill had arranged, intending to perform it — Cage does not know what became of it all. sets and costumes carried to New York, then lost track of Consequences: The project abandoned

Back from his year away in Mexico in early spring 1948, Albers immediately grasps the meaning of what happened in his absence and disapproves: he rejects in particular the courses given by students and the increased emphasis on the social sciences (Molly Gregory: Juppi hated the social sciences; they were a red rag to a bull). More deeply, he believes that Levi, like other newcomers, is trying to take over. Consequences: The Albers/Levi conflict; the college's expansion called into question

According to Dreier, it all began when the Levis moved into the Dreiers' apartment (they were on leave) in “Roadside,” the other half of which the Alberses occupied. The Levis brought disorder into the shared living room — nothing annoys the Alberses more — and Bill Levi supposedly got tangled up with Albers over the upkeep of the furnace: Albers's Westphalian, almost Dutch nature came out, and they soon stopped speaking to each other. the furnace, the shared living room in disorder Consequences: A personal break feeding the institutional conflict
Bolotowsky leaves the community just before the explosion at the end of the summer; he will later judge that nonsense best describes some of the maneuvering around the quarrel over “standards”.

Hired to replace Albers during his leave, he stays until the spring of 1948; tensions with Albers rise, tempered by their shared dislike of Levi. Makes liquor runs to South Carolina in a Studebaker with a rumble seat, Buncombe County being “dry”

A student dares to tell Albers that his matière exercises (fish eggs turned into marbles) are illusionism; furious, Albers has the exhibition room floor varnished too heavily for it to dry before the opening. The matière exercise: making one substance look like something else

Every evening the students fling their leftover paint with a trowel onto a large canvas stretched on the wall of Hebei's room; signed “Anonymous Blotch,” it is hung in the dining hall. Bolotowsky at once identifies each person's palette and is amused; others, who had examined it gravely, feel humiliated. Bolotowsky defends it as a post-Dalí experiment in the Dadaist law of chance, which drives Albers mad with rage — calculated, he says. A canvas described by Jerrold Levy as something between a Motherwell and a de Kooning

Just before the 1948 summer session, Levi supposedly suggested to Bolotowsky that he stay if they tried to oust Albers; Bolotowsky refuses. Duberman found no proof that Levi really wanted to purge the college of his rival.

Hired for a year as M.C. Richards's successor, he writes biblical letters of enthusiasm, then in less than two weeks leaves, disgusted by students who question everything, the homicidal foliage, and rustic life. Albers begs him to stay; he refuses. He arranges for Charles Olson to replace him. The students prefer to believe that he left out of unrequited love for Natasha, who coldly rebuffed him at an evening of wine and waltzes. Works cited: Bottom Dog, Do These Bones Live, Sing Oh Barren, The Flea of Sodom (in progress) Consequences: Olson takes the post

Having sworn never to teach again, Olson agrees, at Dahlberg's insistence, to come three days a month for travel expenses and $120, with “Writing” and “Reading” seminars, evening lectures (non-Homeric myth, Melville), and poetry readings. The three-day agreement is seldom kept: he sometimes skips a month and often stays a week. $120 per visit + travel expenses Consequences: Olson will become the dominant figure at the college until its closing in 1956

Olson's first term as a visitor: his poetry readings and his staging of García Lorca's Lament for Ignacio Sanchez Mejias immediately make him a cult figure; he dominates the community until the closing in 1956. Consequences: Olson becomes the college's strongman until its closing.

Albers tries to expel two nonartist students caught sleeping together one night in the Studies Building; after the girl threatens to post a medical certificate attesting that she is virgo intacta, the two end up staying. Goldowski and Nell Rice were indignant. a certificate of virginity; the scene in the Studies Building. Consequences: Feeds the resentment against Albers.
Interest in Tite's printing course is so great that the class must be split in two, with Frank Rice taking the second group.

Two Australian architects come to Black Mountain with plans (never carried out) for a rammed-earth studio for 600–700 dollars. $600–700; letter from Albers to Milton Rose, Sept. 27, 1948 Consequences: A project never executed

The Lippolds arrive in an old motor hearse; Fuller, delighted, describes it as a beautiful old motor hearse with handsome classical black columns and big windows. Poverty is such that M.C. Richards lends the Lippolds a dime to buy ice cream for their children. a black hearse with classical columns; a dime

Cage proclaims that Beethoven was wrong and that his influence was disastrous for music; Bodky, furious, calls this a “desecration”; the account of the duel comes from the recorded recollections of Jerrold Levy and an interview with Cunningham. Cage asserts that Satie and Webern rediscovered that silence is heard in durations, not in harmony; Beethoven supposedly ran music aground on an island of decadence Consequences: A lasting estrangement, according to the Cage-Goodman version
Albers invites Breuer to come as a “visiting teacher,” but Breuer, too busy, declines any regular commitment. Consequences: The recruitment fails

Dahlberg teaches for two weeks, cannot stand the students' lack of respect, and leaves abruptly, recommending Olson as his replacement; he was then working on Flea of Sodom. Consequences: Olson becomes writing instructor.

An anecdote told by Olson in class: Dahlberg, whose satyr-like impulses were notorious on campus, takes a buxom woman student out to “discuss” her writing and deflowers her during the walk; Rumaker does not know who reported it.

Gorky, physically ill and mentally depressed, kills himself. Bill, shattered, struggles to express his grief: Gorky was like a brother to him; he believes he has lost part of his own life and will always mourn his friend. Bill rejected the idea that Gorky had “influenced” him: Elaine insists that they shared ideas and concerns, drawing on the figure, nature, Surrealism, and European academic painting rather than on pure geometry. Consequences: a lasting grief; that same year, Bill's first solo exhibition: the world changes

In 1948, Bill has his first solo exhibition and enters a new public life; toward the end of the forties he combines colors of close values and biomorphic forms in Surrealist abstractions (Pink Angels, 1947) until about 1950, and pursues until 1949 another series of women. Consequences: he almost makes a living by selling his work

Gorky dies after an illness; Bill, who regarded him as a brother, is devastated and will always grieve for Gorky, talking about him constantly. Consequences: Bill feels he has lost part of his own life

An exhibition that marks the beginning of Bill's rise. MoMA buys Painting, 1948; Art News publishes an enthusiastic review (Renee Arb) and a photo of a canvas; Clement Greenberg calls him one of the four or five most important painters in the country. But almost nothing sells. canvases priced between 300 and 2,000 dollars; the gallery keeps the exhibition open two months longer than planned; nothing sells Consequences: Bill becomes known beyond the New York world; the official start of his public career

After criticizing the mediocrity of the magazine's reviews, Elaine takes up Hess's challenge to do better; she will publish regularly for years and influence two generations of artists. 4 dollars per review Consequences: Elaine's major body of criticism
MoMA acquires a canvas from the Egan exhibition, an institutional consecration. Consequences: Bill known beyond New York

Despite praise, Bill's canvases do not sell; Egan extends the exhibition by two months, nothing sells, general embarrassment. canvases priced between $300 and $2,000; a two-month extension Consequences: The exhibition makes Bill famous and puts him in rivalry with Pollock

Albers, director of the college's art program, sees the reproduction of Bill's painting in Art News and offers him the summer teaching post, with train tickets for Bill and Elaine. $200 for the summer, the train paid for two Consequences: The founding stay of the summer of 1948

Very poor, the de Koonings decide on the train not to rent pillows for the night; a long, hot, slow journey, an exhausted arrival, then wonder at the mountains. rented pillows judged too expensive Consequences: Elaine: “It was heaven”

She acts in a play, attends all of Albers's classes, religiously follows Cunningham's dance classes, and sits in on all of Fuller's. she confides that at 18 she would have given up painting for engineering because of Bucky Consequences: A lifelong admiration for Fuller (lectures of 6 to 8 hours)

For lack of means, she paints in cheap enamel on wrapping paper: drawing abstract forms, viscous color mixed on the surface, drawing with the brush or charcoal in the wet paint, scraping with a palette knife, successive layers. large sheets pinned to the walls; she then regards them as studies Consequences: She comes of age as a painter that summer

Bill praises every student's work, finds something positive everywhere, and advises all those who really want to paint to leave the college for New York; yet he worries about the time stolen from his own painting. works several hours a day in the studio in addition to teaching

Elaine comes back with her rolled-up paintings, moved from studio to studio, almost forgotten; at the end of her life she wants to throw them away (“toss these out”), Lieber insists, and a restoration is arranged with her sister Marjorie. frayed, crumbling edges Consequences: A posthumous exhibition at the Washburn Gallery; the Metropolitan acquires one

Betsy Egan, jealous of everything about Elaine, challenges her to arm wrestling after a very boozy party; a draw after much effort; the two women at once become best friends. Betsy, sturdily built, was heavier and stronger than Elaine; Elaine half drunk, laughing
The issue following the exhibition credits her as an editorial associate; she writes brilliant reviews and keeps Hess and other critics attentive to Bill's work and persona.

In the fall of 1948, Hare, Motherwell, Baziotes, and Rothko found a school named, at Barnett Newman's ironic suggestion, “Subjects of the Artist”; the founders had all exhibited at Peggy Guggenheim's (Art of This Century, 1944-1946), then with Betty Parsons or Sam Kootz. 35 East Eighth Street Consequences: the setting of the Friday lectures that prefigure the Club

A special issue of Life introduces a broad American public to avant-garde art; the public, even when scandalized, takes notice of abstract art, and this visibility, even hostile, becomes attractive to artists. Consequences: Artists begin to prefer being visible to being invisible.

After her apprenticeship with Bill, Elaine spends the summer of 1948 at Black Mountain and commits herself resolutely to abstraction, exploring Abstract Expressionism for ten years. Consequences: The start of a decade of abstract exploration; then a series of sports paintings

Appears on the Art News masthead as an editorial associate; her reviews, admired, combine a fluid vocabulary with precision of thought. She describes photographs as opulent, inks as intricate, charcoals and gouaches as luminous, subtly graded, and warm-toned Consequences: A reputation as an excellent critic among artists

Goodman gives a lecture on Kafka before an audience of students, largely veterans paid by the G.I. Bill; they protest frantically that Kafka is psychotic and has no connection with reality. An audience of veterans on the G.I. Bill; Goodman comments: they had lived through part of The Trial and were then wandering beneath The Castle. Consequences: Illustrates the postwar shock and the conformist retreat of youth.
Richard Lippold takes part in the last summer institute directed by Albers, in 1948, and distinguishes the discipline Albers demanded from the laissez-faire of other progressive schools.

A tumultuous series of events culminates in early summer 1948 in a sharp confrontation between Levi and Albers; Levi resigns as rector and takes a leave. With Ted Dreier refusing to take over the leadership again, Albers becomes rector against his inclination and his better judgment and tackles the fiscal and structural crises. Consequences: Albers rector in spite of himself

Against the background of internal battles, the summer institute organized by Albers is the most fruitful and memorable in the college's history: the legendary summer of Cage, Cunningham, de Kooning, and Fuller, which for many has become the founding moment of Black Mountain. Consequences: A paradoxical artistic peak in the trough of the crisis

After fifteen years, only the Alberses, the Dreiers, and Nell Rice remain of the pioneers of 1933. Anni Albers explains their exhaustion by the constant tension, the constant lack of money, the constant friction with every faculty member holding an equal vote. Anni: “constant tension... constant lack of money... constant friction” Consequences: A feeling that longevity and endurance should count

In the spring 1948 issue of the College Art Journal, Gropius argues for familiar elements of Albers's teaching: knowledge of “visual facts,” experimental workshops, the articulation of Werklehre and Formlehre, priority given to work in three dimensions, work with materials; the pivotal qualities of the design teacher who gives the student confidence and independence.

Shortly before his February speech, Sawyer invites Albers to join the committee to help develop the painting and sculpture program; for lack of enthusiasm for the names of alumni proposed, Albers becomes the only non-Yale member of the committee. Consequences: The beginning of Albers's relationship with Yale, where he will remain an outsider.

Designed by Kahn: the painting and sculpture students in effect embellish a structure created by the architecture students. Consequences: The second collaborative problem (1949-50) will aim at equal responsibility among the members of the team.

Recruiting for Black Mountain's 1948 summer Art Institute, Albers invites Willem de Kooning, whose name had been suggested; de Kooning spends the summer at the college. Consequences: An example of Albers's practice of inviting artists radically different from himself — as long as he kept control

Recruiting for the 1948 summer Institute, Albers invites de Kooning, who has no teaching credentials; he spends the summer at Black Mountain and proves charismatic and popular with the students. Consequences: Albers later invites him as a visiting critic at Yale for two semesters in 1950-51

In the late 1940s, Albers orders packets of Color-aid paper, then containing more than two hundred silkscreened sheets of six by nine inches. more than 200 silkscreened sheets, 6×9 inches Consequences: Provides constant, ready-to-use colors.
Maldonado remembers meeting Scholl and Aicher at Max Bill's in the spring of 1948, when Scholl first mentions her project to Bill Consequences: The genesis of the HfG Ulm

The list of the 1948 summer faculty alone secures the college's mythical status: Willem and Elaine de Kooning, Merce Cunningham, John Cage, Buckminster Fuller, Peter Grippe, Richard Lippold, among others. The student body rises to seventy-seven students, many financed by the GI Bill. Almost none of the summer teachers is paid: given room and board, they enjoy a restful time in the country. Behind the scenes, faculty struggles, alliances, and grudges; the utopian idealism of the early days is fading; an effort is made to suspend disagreements during the summer. 77 students; summer teachers unsalaried, paid in room and board Consequences: the college's identity as an art school consolidated, despite the internal tensions

During the 1948 summer session, Cage organizes a series of evening concerts devoted to Satie's music. Albers, given how rooted the college's musical community is in the Germanic tradition, asks him to give a lecture on Satie's importance. Cage delivers “Defense of Satie,” the first full statement of his personal conception of composition, declaring that only one new idea has appeared since Beethoven, perceptible in Webern and Satie: the parts of a composition are defined not by harmony but by length in time. A lecture following evening concerts; a frontal attack on Beethoven, accused of having killed the art of music Consequences: According to legend, Paul Goodman walked out furious — but Duberman notes that Goodman was not at the college in the summer of 1948: Cage probably merged two memories (the outraged party would have been Bodky).

Cage remembered being indignant at anti-Beethoven remarks, to the point of no longer speaking to their author; but Goodman was not at Black Mountain in the summer of 1948, so Cage merged two separate memories. Cage: “from then on—even to the present day, [we are] not on speaking terms” Consequences: An illustration of the fragile reliability of accounts of the summer of 1948

A first visit in the spring of 1948, which inspires the integration of dance into the program; they come back several times. Consequences: The college then invites the choreographers Katherine Litz and Elizabeth Jennerjahn
A painting made during the summer of 1948, in which de Kooning incorporates collaged elements.

The director of MoMA's department of industrial design offers Albers a solo exhibition; she devotes herself to it from the fall of 1948 until the opening Consequences: MoMA's first solo exhibition devoted to a textile artist
A first meeting during the 1948 summer session, the start of a lifelong friendship. Consequences: In 1949 Fuller grants him a license to develop the Dymaxion principles

During the summer of 1948, Larsen photographs Fuller in his class surrounded by geometric models; he takes her up in a small plane so that she can photograph his failed geodesic dome from the air. a small plane, a bird's-eye view, the dome nicknamed the Supine Dome Consequences: Photographs that have become iconic
Cage, at the college from 1948 on, puts music at the service of projects of moral, spiritual, and psychic self-improvement.

Fuller arrives for his very first teaching post in a three-wheeled camper filled with geometric models. Three wheels, energetic-geometry models Consequences: He quickly wins a fervent following among the students

On the evening of his arrival, despite the grueling drive from New York, Fuller has his aluminum trailer unloaded, full of tetrahedrons, dodecahedrons, icosahedrons, domes, and crystalline pyramids, and gives a three-hour lecture on the coming end of the era of the square and its geodesic future. An aluminum trailer; a three-hour lecture; Lippold: like Zoroaster speaking Islamic; Cunningham: immediate adoration and love Consequences: His studio becomes a cabinet of curiosities, an alchemical laboratory of applied mathematics

Albers invites Cage and Cunningham, warning them that the administration can pay only for the train; once there, Cage has no bed and sleeps on the floor. He does not say where Cunningham slept — they were rather well hidden. Cage's luggage: the 18 existing Satie scores plus the script of his only play, The Ruse of Medusa (1913)

Cage stages Satie's play: slapstick full of puns, with musical interludes danced by a “mechanical monkey” played by Cunningham; Fuller and Elaine de Kooning in the cast; Arthur Penn (the future director) directs; sets by Willem de Kooning, Ray Johnson, Ruth Asawa, among others. Willem de Kooning uses in it a guild secret of trompe-l'œil learned as a teenager in Holland Consequences: A popular success that calms the Beethoven scandal

On a damp morning, after long calculations done by hand (before the computer age), dozens of cheap, flexible venetian-blind slats are assembled as the framework of the first geodesic dome; the dome does not stand up and is humorously nicknamed the Supine Dome. Fuller knew that the slats needed to be doubled but wanted to go along with the principle of progressive reinforcement. Store-bought venetian-blind slats; a photo of Dreier, Lanier, and Elaine de Kooning holding up the dome; Fuller: like confetti Consequences: Illustrates his conviction that tactical failure is an integral part of the experimental method and of educational risk

Willem and Elaine de Kooning come on the strength of the tales of wonder and delight told by Cage and Cunningham, who had visited in the spring of 1947. The invitation comes from Albers, on Cage's recommendation, after Mark Tobey's last-minute withdrawal. Consequences: Elaine attends the classes and takes part in the whole life of the session.

She appears in many archival photos: the failed attempt at Fuller's first geodesic dome, and in costume as Frisette in Erik Satie's The Ruse of Medusa (1913). The role of Frisette; the “Supine Dome” (lying down).

Mark Tobey had just canceled; Cage suggested de Kooning to Albers as a replacement; the sculptor Peter Grippe had already recommended him. De Kooning accepted, glad of an income and a paid getaway. Consequences: The de Koonings spend the summer at BMC, housed in a rustic two-room cottage.

De Kooning painted the sets for Cage's production of The Ruse of Medusa (Satie, 1913) and had long discussions with Fuller; Cunningham remembered the way people from different disciplines could come together and share ideas and conversation.

During the 1948 summer session, Cage organizes an “amateur festival” devoted almost exclusively to the music of Erik Satie: twenty-five evenings of about half an hour each, with Cage himself as the main performer, a pianist of limited means. Albers asked him to give explanatory introductions to the concerts, knowing that it would seem incongruous to the cultivated German émigrés and the followers of Abstract Expressionism. 25 evenings, about 30 minutes each Consequences: These introductions become the lecture “Defense of Satie,” published two decades later.

Cage opens with a sardonic portrait of the solitary modern artist, then rebuilds the foundations of music. Provocations: neoclassicism is an offense against nature; Schoenberg and Stravinsky overrated, purveyors of length and impressiveness; tonal harmony, a residue of Western materialism; and the climax: “Beethoven was in error”. The barb is aimed at Erwin Bodky, an émigré Prussian musicologist, who is then teaching an intensive course on Beethoven's late string quartets. Consequences: The text is published twenty years later in Richard Kostelanetz's anthology.

The Callahans rent the upstairs ballroom of a divided house near Lincoln Park: a single large room, a bathroom, a coat closet turned into a darkroom. Hugo Weber paints playful murals there with a recently introduced quick-drying paint. A darkroom improvised in a closet. Consequences: The setting of many photographs of Eleanor, including Eleanor, Chicago (1949).

Elizabeth Jennerjahn returns in 1948 with her new husband Pete to teach dance; they invent the Light Sound Movement workshops: projected light and movement as independent elements that stimulate each other. Elizabeth describes a rehearsal with Cernovich and Tim La Farge: in their green-and-red striped tights, moving through a saturated red and green light created by red-and-green striped slides. No photographic documentation; the only contemporary account, a notebook of Pete Jennerjahn or Joseph Fiore: two dancers perform simple movements at the two ends of the stage; the lights come on over them alternately. Participants named: Hedden, Cernovich, Don Alter, La Farge, Vera Williams, June Christensen, Richards, Mary Fiore, Dorothea Rockburne, Victor Kalos, Jay Watt, Dan Rice, Frank Moore. green/red striped tights; striped slides; a body appearing and disappearing, an Albers color study in another medium Consequences: prefigure Theater Piece No. 1 and the Merce Cunningham Dance Company

Rauschenberg's first stay, with his wife at the time, Susan Weil. They share the coveted chore of taking the garbage to the dump. According to Weil, they sometimes came back with as much as they had taken Consequences: Lifelong friendships with Merce Cunningham and John Cage; lessons from Josef Albers

Dahlberg lasts only two weeks at Black Mountain; Olson reluctantly agrees to replace him, thus breaking the vow he had made to give up academia. Olson was 37 Consequences: The beginning of his attachment to the college

Shortly after his first visit, Cage writes to Josef and Anni Albers that Black Mountain has shown him that people can still work together, he who believed that what is needed can come about only in each person in isolation. An undated handwritten letter of 1948, preserved at the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation. Consequences: Confirms the fruitfulness of a creative direction (autonomous but connected work) little recognized elsewhere.

Cunningham presents a work titled Orestes; he is known to have been incorporating then into his work a long-standing interest in Native American masks. Native American masks, possible echoes in the forms of Asawa's drawing Dancers. Consequences: A possible influence on the masklike forms in Asawa's drawing Dancers (an interpretation).

A ten-page document written in connection with his resignation, frustrated and bitter but very clear, tracing the college's first 15½ years; preserved in the Walter Gropius collection at the Bauhaus Archive in Berlin. Ten pages Consequences: A major source on the college's history

Albers reluctantly accepts the office of rector of the college in the summer of 1948 and very likely feels bitter about the administrative and development tasks that eat up his time. Consequences: A factor in his departure in 1949

In a funding request to the Whitney Foundation, Albers sets out his plan for reorganizing the college: abandoning the full curriculum of a liberal arts college (which would require at least 30 teachers) to concentrate teaching on the visual arts and music, supplemented by selected academic subjects and practical work. As rector, he was charged with precisely this reorganization, meant to avert future political and financial crises. An estimate: at least 30 teachers for a full liberal arts program Consequences: A vision diverging from that of the founders: training practitioners of the arts rather than teachers of social sciences

Albers makes his first engraving on Vinylite plastic, two years before his departure, which suggests that the resources already existed in North Carolina. Vinylite plastic mounted on a panel Consequences: The beginning of the series of engraved Structural Constellations

Leaves New York by ship in early 1948 and enrolls at the Académie Julian; there he becomes close to the student Susan Weil, his future wife; sees Picassos and Matisses for the first time in Parisian galleries and museums. Each of them thought the other the worst artist in the class Consequences: Their future marriage and their departure together for BMC

In the fall of 1948, Rauschenberg briefly studies with Josef Albers as an auditor at Black Mountain College. It is there that he begins to take an interest in photography and to experiment with photographic means. Consequences: The start of the photographic experiments that will lead to the blueprints of 1949-1951
Studies at the Académie Julian in Paris.

In the summer of 1948, he decides to go to Black Mountain College, a little-known avant-garde school in the mountains of western North Carolina, where Josef Albers heads the fine arts department; he has read in Time that Albers was the greatest disciplinarian in the United States; Weil was already enrolled there. a Time magazine quotation about Albers Consequences: he saves up his fare and joins Weil
He begins his training with Albers in the middle of the fall semester of 1948. an arrival in midsemester Consequences: a fruitful clash of sensibilities with Albers

After reading an article in the August issue of Time on Josef Albers's disciplined approach to art, he enrolls with Susan Weil at Black Mountain College. Despite frequent disagreements, he will later regard Albers as his most important teacher. At the Bauhaus Albers had developed the habit of working with the intrinsic properties of materials and with techniques of “combination” of structure, texture, and facture. An article in Time (the August issue) Consequences: A decisive training

Well before the White Paintings, Cage had proposed a silent composition of three to four minutes, titled Silent Prayer, meant to be broadcast on the radio — which slightly contradicts the official chronology. Title: Silent Prayer; three to four minutes; a radio broadcast planned Consequences: Qualifies the account of a purely pictorial genesis

A combined music and art program organized by Albers. Fuller and de Kooning replace at the last minute invited guests who had canceled. Cage and Cunningham invited after a spring visit. Fuller and his students work on his first geodesic dome, which, failing to rise, is christened the “Supine Dome”; Cage organizes a Satie festival culminating in the first English production of The Ruse of Medusa. The geodesic dome refuses to rise: the “Supine Dome”. Consequences: The college's legendary summer.
In the fall of 1948, Albers invites Olson to replace the departing poet Edward Dahlberg. Consequences: Olson becomes the college's second great leader

Cage arrives at the college with almost all of Erik Satie's 18 existing scores and a copy of Satie's 1913 play “The Ruse of Medusa”. He annoys many of the German émigrés, Albers included, by playing only Satie throughout his stay; a preliminary talk denouncing Beethoven's harmonic tradition in favor of Satie's emphasis on rhythm and duration. 18 Satie scores; the 1913 play Consequences: Tensions with the German émigrés, then rehabilitation thanks to the performance
